claim: Polo-like kinase Cdc5 is required for asymmetric SPB inheritance in S. cerevisiae.
source: Cdc5 inhibition in an asynchronous culture of exponentially growing cells revealed randomized SPB segregation (Figure 1B).
evidence: Experimental data showing randomized SPB segregation upon Cdc5 inhibition in cdc5-as1 cells treated with CMK-C1.

claim: Randomization of SPB fate upon Cdc5 inhibition is not specific to the cdc5-as1 allele.
source: Randomization of SPB fate was also observed when Cdc5 activity was inhibited by shifting cells carrying the cdc5-2 or cdc5-77 thermosensitive alleles at a restrictive temperature (Hu et al., 2001; Ratsima et al., 2016). The results demonstrate that this phenotype is not a specific defect associated with cdc5-as1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Multiple cdc5 alleles (cdc5-2, cdc5-77) show similar SPB inheritance defects, supported by citations to prior work characterizing these alleles.

claim: Spc72 interacts with and is phosphorylated by Cdc5.
source: Spc72 interacts and is phosphorylated by Cdc5 (Maekawa et al., 2007; Snead et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited references provide evidence of Spc72-Cdc5 interaction and phosphorylation.

claim: Spc72-13Myc is post-translationally modified in a cell cycle-dependent manner that peaks in anaphase.
source: In accordance with those data, the Spc72-13Myc fusion protein was increasingly modified post-translationally, peaking in anaphase as the cells synchronously progressed into mitosis, whereas inhibiting Polo-like kinase activity in cdc5-as1 cells markedly impaired the modification (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Western blot analysis showing gel shift of Spc72-13Myc during cell cycle progression.

claim: Inhibiting Cdc5 activity leads to randomization of Spc72-GFP distribution on SPBs.
source: Inhibiting Cdc5 activity in cells from asynchronous culture led to randomization of both Spc72 distribution and SPB fate (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: Microscopy data showing randomized Spc72-GFP localization in cdc5-as1 cells treated with CMK-C1.

claim: Spc72-GFP distribution is randomized in cdc5-2 and cdc5-77 cells at restrictive temperature.
source: Again ruling out an allele-specific defect, Spc72-GFP distribution was also randomized in cdc5-2 and cdc5-77 cells at the restrictive temperature (Figure 1G).
evidence: Microscopy data showing randomized Spc72-GFP in multiple cdc5 mutant alleles.

claim: Cdc5 binding to Spc72 depends on serine residues S231 and S232 in Spc72.
source: Cdc5 binding to Spc72 depends on a binding motif in serine residues S231 and S232 in the Spc72 sequence (Snead et al., 2007).
evidence: Citation to prior work identifying the Cdc5 binding motif in Spc72.

claim: The Spc72-AA mutant protein (S231A, S232A) is randomly distributed during mitosis.
source: Consistent with this, we found that GFP-tagged Spc72-AA mutant protein, in which both serine residues were substituted by alanine (S231A, S232A), was randomly distributed during mitosis in exponentially growing cells (Figure 1G).
evidence: Microscopy data showing randomized Spc72-AA-GFP localization.

claim: Spc72-AA-GFP displays faster electrophoretic mobility than wild-type Spc72-GFP.
source: Similar to that observed for Spc72-GFP in cdc5-as1 cells after the addition of CMK-C1, Spc72-AA-GFP displayed faster electrophoretic mobility than the wild-type Spc72-GFP in the absence of the inhibitor (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: Western blot analysis showing differential migration of Spc72-AA-GFP compared to wild-type.

claim: Lack of Cdc5 activity does not affect the preferential association of Spc72-GFP to the old SPB.
source: However, the lack of Cdc5 activity had hardly any considerable effect on the preferential association of Spc72-GFP to the old SPB (Figure 1C,F).
evidence: Microscopy data showing that Spc72-GFP still preferentially localizes to the old SPB when Cdc5 is inhibited.

claim: Cdc5 acts either downstream or in parallel to Spc72 during establishment of differential SPB inheritance.
source: Therefore, Cdc5 is a determinant of SPB asymmetric segregation that acts either downstream or in parallel to Spc72 during the establishment of the differential SPB inheritance pattern in budding yeast.
evidence: Logical inference from the observation that Cdc5 inhibition does not affect Spc72 preferential association with old SPB but does affect SPB inheritance.

claim: Kar9 asymmetrically loads onto the old SPB during metaphase.
source: Another key factor acting downstream of Spc72 in generating the SPB distribution scheme is Kar9, which asymmetrically loads onto the old SPB during metaphase (Juanes et al., 2013).
evidence: Citation to prior work showing Kar9 asymmetric loading.

claim: Kar9 is transported to microtubule plus ends to bind Myo2, promoting old SPB entrance into the daughter cell.
source: Subsequently, Kar9 is transported to the microtubule plus ends to bind Myo2, a myosin that travels through actin cables toward the bud, promoting old SPB entrance into the daughter cell and establishing the differential SPB fate (Korinek et al., 2000; Liakopoulos et al., 2003; Maekawa et al., 2003; Yin et al., 2000).
evidence: Multiple citations describing the mechanism of Kar9-mediated SPB segregation.

claim: Inhibiting Cdc5-as1 leads to randomization of Kar9-sfGFP loading on SPBs.
source: As with Spc72-GFP, inhibiting Cdc5-as1 also led to randomization of Kar9-sfGFP loading on SPBs in asynchronous cell culture (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Microscopy data showing randomized Kar9-sfGFP distribution upon Cdc5 inhibition.

claim: Lack of Cdc5 activity perturbs the preferential association of Kar9-sfGFP with the old SPB.
source: In contrast, here, the lack of Cdc5 activity perturbed the preferential association of Kar9-sfGFP with the old SPB (Figure 2A,D).
evidence: Microscopy data showing that Kar9-sfGFP does not preferentially localize to old SPB when Cdc5 is inhibited.

claim: An important role of Cdc5 in establishing SPB inheritance is to retain specific loading of Kar9 onto the old SPB.
source: Therefore, an important role of Cdc5 in establishing SPB inheritance is to retain specific loading of Kar9 onto the old SPB.
evidence: Inference from the observation that Cdc5 inhibition disrupts Kar9 preferential association with old SPB.

claim: Cdc5 inhibition causes increased Kar9-sfGFP nuclear retention and localization to interpolar microtubules.
source: Cdc5-as1 inhibition not only disrupted its preferential polarization toward the old SPB and the daughter cell, but also had a severe impact on the overall localization of Kar9. It further caused increased Kar9-sfGFP nuclear retention and localization to the interpolar microtubules (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: Microscopy data showing altered Kar9-sfGFP localization patterns upon Cdc5 inhibition.

claim: Kar9 accumulates slow-migrating forms that are partially dependent on Cdc5 activity.
source: Evaluation of the electrophoretic mobility of 13Myc-tagged Kar9 on polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE) indicated the accumulation of slow-migrating forms of the protein that were partially dependent on Cdc5 activity (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Western blot analysis showing gel shift of Kar9-13Myc that is reduced upon Cdc5 inhibition.

claim: Cdc5 can collaborate in establishing SPB fate by promoting post-translational modifications in Kar9 that control its mobilization from the nucleus and asymmetric distribution to the old SPB.
source: Together, these observations support the premise that Cdc5 can collaborate in establishing SPB fate by promoting post-translational modifications in Kar9 that control its mobilization from the nucleus and its asymmetric distribution to the old SPB.
evidence: Inference from multiple observations about Kar9 modification, localization, and dependence on Cdc5.

claim: Cdc5-as1-eGFP is not observed on SPBs when cells are arrested in G1.
source: In cells simultaneously expressing Cdc5-as1-eGFP and Spc72-mCherry, the eGFP-tagged Cdc5-as1 protein was not observed on the SPBs when cells were arrested in G1 after addition of the α-factor mating pheromone (Figure 3A,B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Microscopy data from synchronized cell cycle experiments showing absence of Cdc5-as1-eGFP on SPBs in G1.

claim: Cdc5-as1-eGFP loads on the old SPB before it is duplicated, and subsequently also on the new SPB.
source: Once the cells were released from the G1 block and allowed to synchronously progress in the cell cycle, Cdc5-as1-eGFP loaded on the old SPB before it was duplicated, and subsequently also on the new SPB.
evidence: Microscopy data from synchronized cell cycle experiments tracking Cdc5-as1-eGFP localization.

claim: Cdc5-as1 remains symmetrically localized on both SPBs until anaphase.
source: Cdc5-as1 remained symmetrically localized on both SPBs until anaphase, finally slowly disappearing as the cells exited mitosis, first from the SPB retained in the mother cell and then from the daughter-inherited SPB (Figure 3A,B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Microscopy data showing symmetric Cdc5-as1-eGFP localization on SPBs during cell cycle progression.

claim: Spc72-mCherry is present on SPBs in cells blocked in G1.
source: In contrast, Spc72-mCherry was already present on the SPBs in cells blocked in G1 (Figure 3A,C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: Microscopy data showing Spc72-mCherry on SPBs in G1-arrested cells.

claim: After SPB duplication, Spc72-mCherry mainly accumulates on the dSPB until late anaphase.
source: Then, once the cells were freed from G1 arrest, and despite the observation of Spc72-mCherry on both SPBs after their duplication, it mainly accumulated on the dSPB, remaining preferentially associated to this SPB until late anaphase, when the protein became more symmetrically distributed (Figure 3A, C–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–E; Juanes et al., 2013).
evidence: Microscopy data showing asymmetric Spc72-mCherry distribution during cell cycle progression, with citation to prior work.

claim: The interaction between Cdc5 and Spc72 is favored on the old SPB.
source: Likewise, the interaction between Cdc5 and Spc72 is favored in the context of the old SPB.
evidence: Inference from BiFC data showing preferential Venus fluorescence on the dSPB.

claim: Inhibiting Cdc5 prevents Spc72-mCherry from symmetrically localizing in anaphase.
source: Additionally, Spc72-mCherry did not symmetrically localize when the cells eventually stopped progressing in anaphase, and instead remained preferentially associated to the dSPB (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: Microscopy data showing persistent asymmetric Spc72-mCherry distribution in late anaphase when Cdc5 is inhibited.

claim: The Spc72-AA-GFP mutant signal is severely reduced on both SPBs.
source: Finally, the signal emitted by the Spc72-AA-GFP mutant was severely reduced on both SPBs and was similar to that of Spc72-GFP on the mother-cell-retained SPB (mSPB) of wild-type cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: Quantitative microscopy data showing reduced Spc72-AA-GFP fluorescence intensity on SPBs.

claim: Lack of Cdc5 activity impedes efficient Spc72 loading on SPBs and prevents its final symmetric association to spindle poles.
source: Our results indicate that the lack of Cdc5 activity impedes efficient Spc72 loading on the SPBs, interfering with the normal Spc72 distribution pattern and preventing its final symmetric association to the spindle poles (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Summary inference from multiple experimental observations about Spc72 loading and distribution.

claim: The Cdc5-Spc72 association is specifically promoted during metaphase-anaphase transition.
source: However, despite both proteins being present on the SPBs before their duplication (Figure 3B,C), the Cdc5–Spc72 association was specifically promoted during metaphase–anaphase transition (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: BiFC data showing Venus fluorescence (indicating Cdc5-Spc72 interaction) appearing during metaphase-anaphase transition.

claim: The Cdc5-Spc72 interaction is preferentially detected on the dSPB.
source: Furthermore, their interaction was preferentially detected on the dSPB, similar to that observed for the differential distribution of Spc72, although the Cdc5–Spc72 association was asymmetrically favored on this SPB for a longer time (Figures 3C and 4E).
evidence: BiFC data showing preferential Venus fluorescence on the dSPB.

claim: The Cdc5-Spc72 interaction is independent of Polo-like kinase activity.
source: Interestingly, although the Cdc5–Spc72 interaction was independent of Polo-like kinase activity, inhibiting Cdc5 compromised their preferential association on the dSPB (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: BiFC data showing that Venus fluorescence still occurs when Cdc5 is inhibited, but the asymmetric distribution is affected.

claim: Cdc5 specifically exerts control on Spc72 during metaphase-anaphase transition.
source: Our results suggest that Cdc5 specifically exerts control on Spc72 during metaphase–anaphase transition.
evidence: Inference from BiFC and cell cycle synchronization experiments.

claim: Inhibiting Cdc5 at metaphase-anaphase transition severely affects the normal Spc72 distribution pattern.
source: First, we preserved Cdc5 activity as cells were released from G1 block into subsequent metaphase arrest caused by conditional inactivation of Cdc20, and then inhibited Cdc5 shortly before Cdc20 was reactivated and cells were allowed to enter anaphase. In these cells, the normal Spc72 distribution pattern remained severely affected, as predicted if Cdc5 were required for the efficient recruitment of Spc72 to SPBs as they transitioned from metaphase to anaphase (Figure 5A,B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Experimental data from conditional Cdc20 inactivation experiments showing that Cdc5 inhibition at metaphase-anaphase transition affects Spc72 distribution.

claim: The normal pattern of Spc72 localization is established when Cdc5 is reactivated shortly before cells enter anaphase.
source: In contrast, and also according to our hypothesis, the regular pattern of Spc72 localization at this cell cycle stage was eventually established when Cdc5 was initially inhibited as the cells progressed from G1 into metaphase arrest, and then reactivated only shortly before they were allowed to advance again into anaphase (Figure 5C,D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: Experimental data from conditional Cdc20 inactivation experiments showing that Cdc5 activity at metaphase-anaphase transition is sufficient for normal Spc72 distribution.

claim: Cdc5 confers SPB identity by modifying Spc72 in the prior cell cycle.
source: This apparent contradiction can be explained if Cdc5 confers SPB identity by modifying Spc72 in the prior cell cycle, so that the consequences of inhibiting Polo-like kinase activity throughout one cell cycle would only be evident during the following division.
evidence: Inference from experiments showing that SPB inheritance is normal in the first cell cycle after Cdc5 inhibition but randomized in subsequent cycles.

claim: SPB inheritance is randomized during the second anaphase in tab6-1 cdc5-as1 cells that enter mitosis from G1 block in the absence of Polo-like kinase activity.
source: Similar to that observed in asynchronous culture, evaluation of the SPB fate in tab6-1 cdc5-as1 cells that synchronously entered mitosis from G1 block in the absence of Polo-like kinase activity indicated that SPB inheritance was randomized during the following anaphase in the cells that managed to escape the initial Cdc5-dependent anaphase arrest and entered a second cell cycle (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Experimental data using tab6-1 bypass mutant showing randomized SPB inheritance in second cell cycle after Cdc5 inhibition.

claim: There is a synergistic effect of Cdc5-as1 inactivation with the spc72-AA mutation on SPB fate.
source: Hence, after pheromone-induced G1 arrest of the cdc5-as1 spc72-AA cells and their subsequent synchronous release in the presence of CMK-C1, we observed a synergistic effect of Cdc5-as1 inactivation with the spc72-AA mutation. This resembled the results during a second cell cycle in our prior synchronization experiments with tab6-1 cdc5-as1 cells. Indeed, while the asymmetric SPB distribution was preserved when Cdc5-as1 was not inhibited, SPB fate was greatly affected as a consequence of the lack of Cdc5 activity in the spc72-AA background (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Experimental data showing enhanced SPB inheritance defects in cdc5-as1 spc72-AA double mutant.

claim: Cdc5 acts as a molecular timer that delays incorporation of new Spc72 onto SPBs until metaphase onset.
source: Hence, Cdc5 would act as a molecular timer that delays the incorporation of new Spc72 onto the SPBs, favoring the interaction of microtubules from the old SPB with the daughter cell cortex and restricting the microtubule nucleation capacity of the new SPB until metaphase onset.
evidence: Inference from multiple experimental observations about timing of Spc72 loading and Cdc5 function.

claim: γ-tubulin (Tub4-mScarlet) preferentially accumulates on the dSPB up to metaphase-anaphase transition.
source: Accordingly, the distribution of γ-tubulin (Tub4-mScarlet), which preferentially accumulates on the dSPB up to metaphase–anaphase transition in an unperturbed cell cycle (Juanes et al., 2013), was randomized when Cdc5 was inhibited, suggesting similar microtubule nucleation capacity of both SPBs under these conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Microscopy data showing Tub4-mScarlet distribution, with citation to prior work.

claim: Transient microtubule depolymerization with nocodazole randomizes SPB fate.
source: However, the transient microtubule depolymerization randomized SPB fate (Figure 6C,D; Pereira et al., 2001).
evidence: Experimental data from nocodazole treatment experiments, with citation to prior work.

claim: Inhibiting Cdc5 activity before cells re-establish the mitotic spindle after nocodazole washout maintains normal SPB inheritance pattern.
source: However, inhibiting Cdc5 activity before the cells were allowed to re-establish the mitotic spindle should prevent new Spc72 molecules from being loaded on the SPBs. Consequently, the old SPB would nucleate more microtubules and thereby be preferentially inherited by the daughter cell. In accordance with this prediction, Spc72 remained preferentially loaded on the dSPB, and the normal SPB inheritance pattern was maintained when cdc5-as1 cells were released from nocodazole arrest in the presence of CMK-C1 (Figure 6F–H).
evidence: Experimental data from nocodazole washout experiments showing that Cdc5 inhibition prevents randomization of SPB fate.

claim: cdc5-16 cells display a subtler defect in asymmetric SPB distribution than cdc5 mutants with impaired kinase activity.
source: cdc5-16 cells displayed a subtler defect in asymmetric SPB distribution than cdc5 mutants with impaired kinase activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Experimental data comparing SPB inheritance defects in different cdc5 mutants.

claim: Neither Kar9 distribution nor its post-translational modification pattern are perturbed in cdc5-16 cells.
source: In this way, and supporting the premise that Cdc5 localization to SPBs is not essential for establishing their fate, neither Kar9 distribution (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) nor its post-translational modification pattern (Figure 2H) were perturbed in cdc5-16 cells.
evidence: Experimental data showing normal Kar9 distribution and modification in cdc5-16 mutant.

claim: Spc72 distribution and loading to SPBs are severely affected in cdc5-16 cells.
source: However, Spc72 distribution and loading to SPBs were severely affected in those conditions, with both spindle MTOCs exhibiting significantly reduced Spc72 levels (Figures 1G and 3F).
evidence: Experimental data showing reduced Spc72 levels on SPBs in cdc5-16 mutant.

claim: Both Cdc5 activity and loading to SPBs are required for promoting Spc72 targeting to these structures.
source: These results indicate that while both Cdc5 activity and loading to SPBs are required for promoting Spc72 targeting to these structures, only the kinase activity is essential for fostering the pivotal role of Kar9 in maintaining the pre-determined SPB inheritance pattern.
evidence: Inference from comparison of phenotypes in different cdc5 mutants.

claim: The loss of Cdc5-dependent regulation of Kar9 has more detrimental consequences on SPB fate determination than that of Spc72.
source: These observations also suggest that the loss of Cdc5-dependent regulation of Kar9 has more detrimental consequences on SPB fate determination than that of Spc72.
evidence: Inference from comparison of SPB inheritance defects in different mutant backgrounds.

claim: Lack of Kar9 leads to randomized SPB segregation.
source: According to its pivotal role in establishing the SPB inheritance pattern, and as previously observed (Moore et al., 2006; Pereira et al., 2001), the lack of Kar9 led to randomized SPB segregation (Figure 7A).
evidence: Experimental data from kar9Δ cells, with citations to prior work.

claim: KAR9 deletion does not interfere with Spc72 loading and preferential association to the old SPB.
source: In contrast, KAR9 deletion did not interfere with Spc72 loading and preferential association to the old SPB (Figure 7B,C), in agreement with Spc72 acting upstream of Kar9 (Juanes et al., 2013).
evidence: Experimental data showing normal Spc72 distribution in kar9Δ cells, with citation to prior work.

claim: SPC72 deletion randomizes SPB inheritance.
source: SPC72 deletion, which is viable in the W303 background (Hoepfner et al., 2002), also randomized SPB inheritance (Figure 7D).
evidence: Experimental data from spc72Δ cells, with citation to prior work on viability.

claim: The lack of Spc72 severely affects Kar9 loading on SPBs.
source: However, the lack of Spc72 severely affected Kar9 loading on the SPBs (Figure 7E,F), which indicates that a pivotal role of Spc72 in determining SPB fate is mediating Kar9 recruitment to these structures.
evidence: Experimental data showing reduced Kar9 on SPBs in spc72Δ cells.

claim: The lack of Kar9 binding to SPBs in the absence of Spc72 is not due to protein degradation.
source: The lack of Kar9 binding to SPBs in the absence of Spc72 was not due to protein degradation (Figure 7G).
evidence: Western blot data showing Kar9 protein levels in spc72Δ cells.

claim: Kar9 is still post-translationally modified in spc72Δ cells.
source: Furthermore, Kar9 was still post-translationally modified in spc72Δ cells (Figure 7G), which agrees with our earlier observations, suggesting that Cdc5 likely regulates Kar9 function by promoting its modification in the nucleus and thereby controlling its capacity to be mobilized from this cellular compartment to associate with the old SPB and to polarize toward the daughter cell (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Western blot data showing Kar9 gel shift in spc72Δ cells, combined with inference about Cdc5 function.

claim: Both Kar9-13Myc and Tub4-mScarlet co-immunoprecipitate with Spc72-GFP.
source: In accordance with our hypothesis, our analyses demonstrated that both Kar9-13Myc and Tub4-mScarlet co-immunoprecipitated with Spc72-GFP and that the interaction efficiency decreased when the Spc72-AA-GFP mutant was expressed instead of the wild-type Spc72 or when the cdc5-as1 allele inhibited Cdc5 activity (Figure 7H,I, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data showing Kar9 and Tub4 interaction with Spc72.

claim: Cdc5 inhibition increases the number of cells showing opposite preferential distribution of Kar9-GFP and Spc72-mCherry.
source: Cdc5 inhibition duplicated the number of cells that showed opposite preferential distribution of Kar9-GFP and Spc72-mCherry (Figure 7J–L).
evidence: Microscopy data showing increased opposite distribution of Kar9 and Spc72 upon Cdc5 inhibition.

claim: Lack of Polo-like kinase activity has greater impact on Kar9 distribution when Spc72 is correctly localized than on Spc72 distribution when Kar9 is correctly localized.
source: Furthermore, the lack of Polo-like kinase activity had a greater impact on the percentage of cells that displayed an inverted Kar9 distribution pattern when Spc72 was correctly localized than on the number of cells in which Spc72 distribution was reversed but Kar9 was localized as in the wild-type. This supports the idea that Cdc5 regulates both Spc72 loading on SPBs and the association of Kar9 with Spc72 and the old SPB (Figure 7L).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of coincidental vs. opposite distribution patterns of Kar9 and Spc72.

claim: The preferential bias of Spc72 toward the old SPB is maintained in cdc5-as1 tab6-1 cells entering a second cell cycle in the presence of CMK-C1.
source: In agreement with new Spc72 loading being dependent on Cdc5 activity, the preferential bias that Spc72 showed toward the old SPB was maintained after cdc5-as1 tab6-1 cells synchronized in G1 were allowed to enter a second cell cycle in the presence of CMK-C1, despite SPB fate being randomized as a result of Polo-like kinase inhibition (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Experimental data from tab6-1 bypass experiments showing maintained Spc72 asymmetry in second cell cycle.

claim: Kar9 association to the old SPB is impaired in cdc5-as1 tab6-1 cells entering a second cell cycle.
source: However, while Kar9 preferential loading on the old SPB was not affected when cells synchronously progressed through mitosis in the presence of CMK-C1 after initial G1 arrest (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F,G), Kar9 association to the old SPB was impaired in cdc5-as1 tab6-1 cells that managed to enter a second cell cycle (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Experimental data comparing Kar9 distribution in first vs. second cell cycle after Cdc5 inhibition.

claim: Kar9 remains preferentially associated to the old SPB after nocodazole block.
source: Moreover, in contrast to Spc72, Kar9 remained preferentially associated to the old SPB in the return-to-growth experiment after nocodazole block (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: Experimental data from nocodazole washout experiments showing maintained Kar9 asymmetry.

claim: Cdc5 facilitates timely and sequential recruitment of Spc72 to the SPBs and confers each SPB its identity during mitosis.
source: Overall, our results support a model in which Cdc5 facilitates timely and sequential recruitment of Spc72 to the SPBs, confers each SPB its identity during mitosis, and promotes the specific association of Kar9 to the old SPB (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Summary inference from all experimental observations presented in the study.

claim: Spc72 has a central role in conferring the SPB the capacity to nucleate microtubules.
source: Spc72 has a central role in conferring the SPB the capacity to nucleate microtubules (Knop and Schiebel, 1998).
evidence: Citation to prior work on Spc72 function.

claim: Cdc5 phosphorylates Spc72 both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Although Cdc5 phosphorylates Spc72 both in vitro and in vivo, the precise regulatory function of the phosphorylation has not been characterized (Maekawa et al., 2007; Snead et al., 2007).
evidence: Citations to prior work showing Cdc5-mediated Spc72 phosphorylation.

claim: Efficient loading of new Spc72 molecules on SPBs requires both Cdc5 activity and its presence on these structures.
source: Here, analyses of the dynamics of Cdc5 and Spc72 localization during the cell cycle demonstrated that the efficient loading of new Spc72 molecules on the SPBs requires both Cdc5 activity and its presence on these structures, and that it is only dynamically promoted once cells reach metaphase–anaphase transition.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from cell cycle synchronization and localization studies.

claim: Spc72 is loaded on SPBs in a mainly conservative manner.
source: As Spc72 is loaded on the SPBs in a mainly conservative manner (Lengefeld et al., 2018), delaying Spc72 recruitment up to metaphase–anaphase transition determines that microtubule nucleation from the old SPB, and therefore preferential anchoring of the old SPB to the daughter cell cortex (Juanes et al., 2013), is initially favored over that from the new one.
evidence: Citation to prior work on Spc72 loading mechanism, combined with inference about functional consequences.

claim: The final symmetric localization of Spc72 guarantees that every cell will carry it on the old SPB as they enter the subsequent cell cycle.
source: On the other hand, the final symmetric localization of Spc72 guarantees that every cell will carry it on the old SPB as they enter the subsequent cell cycle.
evidence: Inference about the functional significance of symmetric Spc72 distribution in late anaphase.

claim: Cdc5 activity not only facilitates Spc72 recruitment on SPBs, but also contributes to bestowing the old SPB its identity during the next cell cycle.
source: Finally, and importantly, our results support the premise that Cdc5 activity not only facilitates Spc72 recruitment on the SPBs, but also contributes to bestowing the old SPB its identity during the next cell cycle.
evidence: Summary inference from experiments showing effects across multiple cell cycles.

claim: Cdc5 likely enables asymmetric Kar9 distribution to the old SPB by directly promoting specific cell cycle-dependent post-translational modifications of Kar9.
source: Our results suggest that Cdc5 likely enables asymmetric Kar9 distribution to the old SPB by directly promoting specific cell cycle–dependent post-translational modifications of this protein.
evidence: Inference from observations of Kar9 modification patterns and their dependence on Cdc5.

claim: Only Cdc5 activity, but not its localization on SPBs, is essential for promoting the pivotal role of Kar9 in maintaining the SPB inheritance pattern.
source: In contrast to Spc72, only Cdc5 activity, but not its localization on the SPBs, is essential for promoting the pivotal role of Kar9 in maintaining the SPB inheritance pattern.
evidence: Comparison of phenotypes in different cdc5 mutants affecting kinase activity vs. localization.

claim: Kar9 is ubiquitylated in the nucleus.
source: Kar9 is ubiquitylated in the nucleus, where many processes involving SUMO modification also occur, and signaling from kinetochores is important for Kar9 trafficking between the nucleus and cytoplasm and for establishing its asymmetric distribution (Leisner et al., 2008; Schweiggert et al., 2016).
evidence: Citations to prior work on Kar9 modification and trafficking.

claim: Kar9 sumoylation is controlled by an unknown pathway that is downregulated by the spindle assembly checkpoint.
source: Kar9 sumoylation is controlled by, among other factors, an unknown pathway that is downregulated by the spindle assembly checkpoint (Leisner et al., 2008), and Cdc5 is a central target of the main mitotic checkpoints (Hu and Elledge, 2002; Valerio-Santiago et al., 2013).
evidence: Citations to prior work on Kar9 sumoylation and Cdc5 regulation by checkpoints.

claim: The role of Cdc5 in controlling Kar9 function in asymmetric SPB inheritance is exerted in the nucleus and not on the SPBs.
source: In agreement with these observations, our data support the premise that the role of Cdc5 in controlling Kar9 function in asymmetric SPB inheritance is exerted in the nucleus and not on the SPBs.
evidence: Inference from observations that Cdc5 localization to SPBs is not required for Kar9 function.

claim: Within the nucleus, Cdc5 mediates post-translational modifications of Kar9, regulating its mobilization from the nucleus and its asymmetric distribution to the old SPB.
source: Within the nucleus, Cdc5 mediates post-translational modifications of Kar9, regulating its mobilization from the nucleus and its asymmetric distribution to the old SPB and polarization toward the daughter cell.
evidence: Inference from observations of Kar9 nuclear retention and modification patterns upon Cdc5 inhibition.

claim: Kar9 localization to SPBs is completely dependent on Spc72.
source: We demonstrate that Kar9 localization to SPBs is completely dependent on Spc72 and that the association between Kar9 and Spc72 is reduced in the absence of Cdc5 activity.
evidence: Experimental data showing loss of Kar9 on SPBs in spc72Δ cells and reduced co-immunoprecipitation upon Cdc5 inhibition.

claim: The specific interaction of Cdc5 and Spc72 on the dSPB is compromised by the lack of Cdc5 activity.
source: Furthermore, we show that the specific interaction of Cdc5 and Spc72 on the dSPB is compromised by the lack of Cdc5 activity, and that Cdc5 inactivation leads to an increase in the cells that display opposed asymmetric distribution of Spc72 and Kar9 on the SPBs.
evidence: BiFC data and microscopy data showing altered Cdc5-Spc72 interaction and Spc72-Kar9 co-distribution upon Cdc5 inhibition.

claim: A final contribution of Cdc5 to SPB fate determination is regulating the association of Kar9 and Spc72 to favor Kar9 loading on the old SPB.
source: This evidence suggests that a final contribution of Cdc5 to SPB fate determination is regulating the association of Kar9 and Spc72 to favor Kar9 loading on the old SPB.
evidence: Inference from multiple observations about Kar9-Spc72 interaction and its dependence on Cdc5.

claim: Cdc5 controls Spc72 recruitment to SPBs in the methylotrophic yeast Ogataea polymorpha.
source: Cdc5 also controls Spc72 recruitment to SPBs in the methylotrophic yeast Ogataea polymorpha, even though there is uncertainty about whether SPB inheritance is asymmetric in this organism and the differential regulation displayed by Spc72 between both yeasts (Maekawa et al., 2017).
evidence: Citation to prior work on Cdc5 function in O. polymorpha.

claim: Cdc5 acts as a molecular timer that promotes preferential segregation of the old SPB into the daughter cell by controlling the temporal pattern of distribution of both Spc72 and Kar9 during the cell cycle.
source: In summary, the evidence collected clearly defines a functional link between Cdc5, Spc72, and Kar9 in SPB fate establishment in S. cerevisiae that supports a model in which Cdc5 acts as a molecular timer that promotes the preferential segregation of the old SPB into the daughter cell by controlling the temporal pattern of distribution of both Spc72 and Kar9 during the cell cycle (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Summary of the main model proposed based on all experimental findings.

claim: Cdc5 determines SPB fate by restricting localization of Spc72 to the old SPB, providing differential microtubule nucleation capacity to each spindle pole.
source: In this way, Cdc5 determines SPB fate by restricting localization of Spc72 to the old SPB, providing a differential microtubule nucleation capacity to each spindle pole.
evidence: Inference about the mechanism by which Cdc5 controls SPB fate through Spc72.

claim: Cdc5 promotes Kar9 mobilization from the nucleus, its asymmetric recruitment to the old SPB, and its polarization toward the daughter cell.
source: Additionally, Cdc5 promotes Kar9 mobilization from the nucleus, its asymmetric recruitment to the old SPB, and its polarization toward the daughter cell, stabilizing the microtubule array from the old spindle MTOC and ensuring its segregation toward the daughter cell (Lengefeld et al., 2018).
evidence: Summary of Cdc5 functions in Kar9 regulation, with citation.

claim: Cdc5 fine-tunes the asymmetric distribution of the old SPB into the bud by regulating the association of Spc72 and Kar9.
source: Furthermore, Cdc5 fine-tunes the asymmetric distribution of the old SPB into the bud by also regulating the association of Spc72 and Kar9.
evidence: Inference from observations about Spc72-Kar9 interaction and its dependence on Cdc5.

claim: Cdc5 is required for proper establishment of SPB identity during mitosis to ensure asymmetric segregation of the old SPB can be maintained during the subsequent cell cycle.
source: Finally, Cdc5 is required for the proper establishment of SPB identity during mitosis to ensure that the asymmetric segregation of the old SPB can be maintained during the subsequent cell cycle.
evidence: Inference from experiments showing effects of Cdc5 inhibition across multiple cell cycles.

claim: Cdc5 could confer SPB identity by modifying Spc72 so that it facilitates the preferential interaction of Spc72 and Kar9 during the following cell cycle.
source: As Cdc5 regulates Spc72–Kar9 association, a distinct possibility is that it could confer SPB identity by modifying Spc72 so that it facilitates the preferential interaction of Spc72 and Kar9 during the following cell cycle.
evidence: Speculation about the mechanism by which Cdc5 confers SPB identity.

claim: Other factors likely collaborate with Cdc5 in establishing Spc72 asymmetric localization by promoting the interaction of both proteins on the old SPB.
source: Despite Cdc5 being present on both SPBs after their duplication, its association with Spc72 is favored on the old SPB. Hence, other factors are likely to collaborate with Cdc5 in establishing Spc72 asymmetric localization by promoting the interaction of both proteins on the old SPB, facilitating the differential modification and specific cellular destiny of Spc72.
evidence: Inference from the observation that Cdc5 is on both SPBs but interacts preferentially with Spc72 on the old SPB.

claim: Swe1 kinase is a candidate factor that collaborates with Cdc5 in establishing SPB fate.
source: One candidate is the Swe1 kinase, which contributes to SPB fate establishment during G1 at least in part through the phosphorylation of Nud1, an integral SPB component that anchors Spc72 (Lengefeld et al., 2017).
evidence: Citation to prior work on Swe1 function, combined with speculation about its collaboration with Cdc5.

claim: Spc72 and Nud1 interaction is modulated via changes in their phosphorylation status, which both depend on Cdc5.
source: Spc72 and Nud1 interaction is modulated via changes in their phosphorylation status, which both depend on Cdc5 (Gruneberg et al., 2000; Lengefeld et al., 2017; Park et al., 2008).
evidence: Citations to prior work on Spc72-Nud1 interaction and its regulation.

claim: The concerted action of Cdc5 and Swe1 could favor the preferential interaction of Nud1, Spc72, and Cdc5 in the old SPB.
source: The concerted action of Cdc5 and Swe1 could favor the preferential interaction of Nud1, Spc72, and Cdc5 in the old SPB and the specific association of Spc72 and Kar9 on this particular spindle MTOC, ensuring tight control of SPB inheritance.
evidence: Speculation about how Cdc5 and Swe1 might work together.

claim: The Cdc5-Spc72 interaction follows the same temporal pattern as that previously described for Swe1 and Nud1.
source: Accordingly, the Cdc5–Spc72 interaction follows the same temporal pattern as that previously described for Swe1 and Nud1 (Lengefeld et al., 2017).
evidence: Comparison of temporal patterns with citation to prior work.

claim: CDK Cdc28 is another potential candidate for aiding Cdc5 in conferring specific cellular fate to each SPB.
source: Another potential candidate for aiding Cdc5 in conferring a specific cellular fate to each SPB is the cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) Cdc28.
evidence: Speculation about potential role of CDK in SPB fate determination.

claim: CDK-dependent Kar9 phosphorylation is important for its asymmetric distribution on SPBs.
source: CDK-dependent Kar9 phosphorylation is important for its asymmetric distribution on SPBs (Liakopoulos et al., 2003; Maekawa and Schiebel, 2004; Moore and Miller, 2007).
evidence: Citations to prior work on CDK-mediated Kar9 phosphorylation.

claim: Phosphorylation of certain substrates by Cdc5 requires prior phosphorylation of a POLO-binding domain in the targeted protein by CDK.
source: Phosphorylation of certain substrates by Cdc5 requires prior phosphorylation of a POLO-binding domain in the targeted protein by CDK (Elia et al., 2003).
evidence: Citation to prior work on priming phosphorylation for Polo-like kinase substrates.

claim: CDK-mediated Kar9 phosphorylation could subsequently favor its Cdc5-dependent regulation.
source: Hence, CDK-mediated Kar9 phosphorylation could subsequently favor its Cdc5-dependent regulation.
evidence: Speculation about potential mechanism linking CDK and Cdc5 in Kar9 regulation.

claim: Differential spindle MTOC inheritance patterns have been described in neuroblasts and glia progenitor cells from different organisms.
source: Differential spindle MTOC inheritance patterns have been described in neuroblasts and glia progenitor cells from different organisms, establishing a link between non-random centrosome distribution and brain development.
evidence: General statement about prior observations in the field.

claim: During Drosophila neuroblast asymmetric division, the centrosome containing the daughter centriole acts initially as the only functional MTOC.
source: During Drosophila neuroblast asymmetric division, the centrosome that contains the daughter centriole acts initially as the only functional MTOC and remains stationary, while the centrosome carrying the mother centriole is maintained in an inactive state and does not become proficient as a MTOC until it moves to the opposite side of the cell, which allows the neuroblast to specifically retain the daughter centriole (Januschke et al., 2011; Rusan and Peifer, 2007).
evidence: Citations to prior work on Drosophila neuroblast centrosome behavior.

claim: Differential centrosome behavior in Drosophila neuroblasts depends on the capacity of POLO to phosphorylate centrobin (CNB).
source: This process depends on the capacity of POLO to phosphorylate the centrosomal protein centrobin (CNB) (Januschke et al., 2013).
evidence: Citation to prior work on POLO function in Drosophila neuroblasts.

claim: Neuroblasts expressing a mutant CNB protein that cannot be phosphorylated by POLO retain some specific daughter centriole binding.
source: However, neuroblasts expressing a mutant CNB protein that cannot be phosphorylated by POLO retain some specific daughter centriole binding, suggesting that this kinase targets other centrosomal proteins to facilitate their differential behavior (Januschke et al., 2013).
evidence: Citation to prior work suggesting additional POLO targets beyond CNB.

claim: Both POLO and Cnn localize to the centrosome that retains nucleation activity in Drosophila neuroblasts.
source: Interestingly, both POLO and Cnn, the Drosophila homologue of Spc72 and human CDK5RAP2, localize to the centrosome that retains nucleation activity (Rusan and Peifer, 2007).
evidence: Citation to prior work on POLO and Cnn localization in Drosophila.

claim: POLO regulates centrosome maturation in Drosophila syncytial embryos and human HeLa S3 cells by controlling Cnn and CDK5RAP2 activity.
source: Furthermore, POLO regulates centrosome maturation in Drosophila syncytial embryos and human HeLa S3 cells by controlling Cnn and CDK5RAP2 activity, respectively, although a direct link between this phenomenon and the specification of a differential centrosome fate has not been established (Conduit et al., 2014; Hanafusa et al., 2015).
evidence: Citations to prior work on POLO regulation of centrosome maturation.

claim: γ-TuCRs from the Spc72 family are exceptional candidates as mediators of Polo-like kinase function during asymmetric centrosome/SPB distribution.
source: Based on our results, γ-TuCRs from the Spc72 family are exceptional candidates as mediators of Polo-like kinase function during asymmetric centrosome/SPB distribution.
evidence: Inference from the current study's findings about Spc72 and Cdc5, extrapolated to other organisms.

claim: Correct centrosome orientation in Drosophila male GSCs depends on Apc2, the Kar9 and mammalian APC homolog.
source: Correct centrosome orientation in Drosophila male GSCs depends on Apc2, the Kar9 and mammalian adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) homolog (Inaba et al., 2010; Yamashita et al., 2003).
evidence: Citations to prior work on Apc2 function in Drosophila GSCs.

claim: APC regulates spindle asymmetry in mouse gut epithelium.
source: Furthermore, APC regulates spindle asymmetry in mouse gut epithelium (Quyn et al., 2010), and mammalian APC preferentially localizes to the mother centriole (Louie et al., 2004).
evidence: Citations to prior work on APC function in mammalian cells.

claim: A key phosphorylation site for Kar9 asymmetric localization to SPBs is conserved in APC.
source: A key phosphorylation site for Kar9 asymmetric localization to SPBs is conserved in APC (Trzepacz et al., 1997).
evidence: Citation to prior work on conserved phosphorylation sites.

claim: It would be interesting to analyze whether Plk1 can control APC localization in human cells.
source: Hence, it would be extremely interesting to analyze whether Plk1 can also control APC localization in human cells, particularly considering that most sporadic colon cancers are attributable to APC mutations (Thenappan et al., 2009).
evidence: Speculation about potential future research directions, with citation about APC and cancer.

claim: Defects in spindle orientation or centrosome distribution during asymmetric cell division are linked with accelerated aging and development of cancer and neurodegenerative disorders.
source: Precise understanding of how differential spindle MTOC inheritance is regulated is of utmost importance, especially because the evidence establishes a link between defects in spindle orientation or centrosome distribution during asymmetric cell division with accelerated aging and the development of cancer and neurodegenerative disorders (Cheng et al., 2008; Knoblich, 2010; Lancaster and Knoblich, 2012; Manzano-López et al., 2019).
evidence: Citations to prior work linking spindle/centrosome defects to disease.
